text: Run this on Azure Quantum can mean three genuinely different things: run it on a simulator, project what it would cost on future fault-tolerant hardware, or run it on an actual physical quantum processor today. Picking the wrong one for the stage you're at wastes either your time or real money.

Every target falls into one of three categories, and the submission code looks almost identical across all three — you select a different target string and the same workspace.submit call routes the job appropriately. A simulator computes the exact result by tracking the state vector in classical memory — what you've used since Chapter 1. The resource estimator, covered next lesson, doesn't run your program at all — it projects what running it would cost on future fault-tolerant hardware. And real hardware means actual third-party quantum processors, with today's real noise and queue times.

A common misconception is that Azure Quantum is one Microsoft-built quantum computer. It isn't. Microsoft supplies the workspace, the Q# tooling, and the resource estimator — the physical processors come from separate hardware partners. IonQ's trapped-ion systems reach up to thirty-six qubits on their Forte generation. Quantinuum's System Model H2, also trapped-ion, offers up to thirty-two fully connected qubits with qubit reuse. Rigetti's superconducting Cepheus-1 processor reaches one hundred eight qubits. Because this is a marketplace, your Q# code and resource-estimation workflow stay the same even as which hardware partners are available changes.

A realistic project moves through these targets in order. Start with a local or cloud simulator while you're writing and debugging the algorithm itself — cheap, fast, exact ground truth. Move to the resource estimator once the algorithm is correct, to check whether it's even feasible on hardware that doesn't exist yet. Only move to real hardware once you have a specific reason — research into error rates, demonstrating a result on physical qubits, validating a noise-mitigation strategy. Running straight to real hardware before validating on a simulator is a common, expensive mistake: you wait in queue for a job that was going to fail anyway, and noisy output makes a logic bug and a hardware error look identical.

Next lesson goes deep on the second of those three categories — exactly what the resource estimator computes, what you feed it, and a worked illustrative calculation showing where its numbers actually come from.
